It has been said that they are the stars that move in their courses, all of which have motion, though they differ in speed and slowness, as is explained in its place. It has been said that they are the seven famous planets, called the wandering stars (al-sayyara). It has been said that al-Dhariyat are fertile women, for they scatter children, as if the succession of children is likened to what is blown away by the winds. The rest of the terms, as I have heard earlier, are in the same sequence. It has been said that al-Dhariyat are the causes which scatter creatures, likening the causes prepared for emergence from non-existence to the winds that scatter grains and the like. It has been said that al-Hamilat are the winds which carry the clouds. It has been said that they are the causes which carry their effects metaphorically. It has been said that al-Jariyat are the winds flowing in their directions. It has been said that al-Muqassimat are the clouds, by which Allah Most High distributes the provisions of His servants. It has been said that they are the seven wandering stars, which is a false view, held only by one who claims that they govern the world of generation and corruption. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Qatada: "Allah Most High created these stars for three purposes: He made them an adornment for the heaven, missiles against the devils, and signs by which one is guided. Razin added: "and what he has no knowledge of, and what the prophets and angels were unable to know." From al-Rabiʿ the same is related, with the addition: "By Allah, Allah did not place in any star the life of anyone, nor his provision, nor his death; they only fabricate lies against Allah and make excuses by the stars." This was mentioned by the author of Jami al-Usul. The discussion refuting what the astrologers claimed has already passed in detail, so recall it. Perhaps something of that will come later, God willing. It is also permissible that all of these be taken to refer to the winds, for they, as they scatter, and what they scatter, stir up the clouds and carry them, flowing through the air with ease, and distributing the rain by directing the clouds to the regions. The reliance is upon what was related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, hearing it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and what the gate of the city of knowledge, may Allah honour his face, said from the pulpit. To this, as has been reported from al-Zajjaj, all the commentators, meaning the authoritative ones, have gone. The statement of the Imam after quoting it from the Amir: "The closest view is that bearing these four attributes on the winds is a great audacity, not to be accepted, and an ignorance of what Ibn al-Musayyab related, a report indicating that this is the interpretation of the Prophet (ﷺ)." Where is the Imam compared with ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him?

The statement of the author of al-Kashf: "It is highly suitable to the context, and for this reason the Imam preferred it," I do not accept for him either, if the hadith is sound. Then, if these attributes are taken to refer to different, distinct matters, as in the view relied upon, then the fa' (then) indicates order in the oaths both in mention and in rank, according to the gradation of their levels in indicating the perfection of His power, Mighty and Majestic. This gradation is either ascending or descending, since each of them has attributes which make it higher in one respect and lower in another when viewed by a sound observer. It has been said that the order is by reference to what is nearer to us and then what is nearer. If, however, all are taken to refer to one thing, namely the winds, then the order is that of the actions and attributes, for the wind first scatters the vapours into the air until they coalesce into cloud; second, it carries it; third, it moves with it, spreading and driving it to where Allah Most High commands, and then it distributes its rain. It has been said that if al-Dhariyat and al-Hamilat are taken to refer to women, then the apparent sense is that they differ in the indication of the perfection of power; so reflect.

The accusative of ﴿dharwan﴾ is as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), and ﴿wiqran﴾ is as a direct object (maf'ul bihi). Al-Imam permitted that it be of the type of "I struck him with a whip" (where the instrument is the object). ﴿Yusran﴾ is an attribute of an elided verbal noun with an elided genitive, meaning gliding with ease, or it is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning made easy, as related from Sibawayh. ﴿Amran﴾ is a direct object and is the singular of "affairs"; the singular is used for the plural, and it was not expressed in plural because the singular suits the rhyme endings, along with the clarity of the matter. It has been said that it is a circumstantial accusative, meaning commanded, with the direct object elided, or the attribute is treated as an intransitive, meaning that they perform the distribution commanded. Abu ʿAmr and Hamza read ﴿wa-l-dhariyati dharwan﴾ with the assimilation of the taʾ into the dhal. It is also read "wiqran" with a fatha on the waw, as a verbal noun of waqara, meaning to carry, as the words of al-Zamakhshari indicate, and sufficient is he as an imam in the language. Accordingly, it is also an object in the sense of the thing carried, or an absolute object of al-hamilat, as if it were said: "then the carriers carry a load."

He said: They are the ships. Were it not that I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say it, I would not have said it. He said: Then tell me about ﴿those that distribute the affair﴾. He said: They are the angels. Were it not that I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say it, I would not have said it. Then he ordered that he be beaten a hundred times and confined in a house. When he recovered, he summoned him and beat him another hundred times, put him on a saddle, and wrote to Abu Musa al-Ashʿari: Prevent the people from sitting with him. In a report from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hamilat are ships laden with people and their goods. It has also been said that they are all carriers of every kind of animal. It has been said that al-Jariyat are the clouds that flow and move wherever Allah, Mighty and Majestic, wills. It has been said that they are the stars that move in their courses, all of which have motion, though they differ in speed and slowness, as is explained in its place. It has been said that they are the seven famous planets, called the wandering stars (al-sayyara). It has been said that al-Dhariyat are fertile women, for they scatter children, as if the succession of children is likened to what is blown away by the winds. The rest of the terms, as I have heard earlier, are in the same sequence. It has been said that al-Dhariyat are the causes which scatter creatures, likening the causes prepared for emergence from non-existence to the winds that scatter grains and the like. It has been said that al-Hamilat are the winds which carry the clouds. It has been said that they are the causes which carry their effects metaphorically. It has been said that al-Jariyat are the winds flowing in their directions. It has been said that al-Muqassimat are the clouds, by which Allah Most High distributes the provisions of His servants. It has been said that they are the seven wandering stars, which is a false view, held only by one who claims that they govern the world of generation and corruption. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Qatada: "Allah Most High created these stars for three purposes: He made them an adornment for the heaven, missiles against the devils, and signs by which one is guided. Whoever interprets them otherwise has erred, wasted his share, and burdened himself with what he has no knowledge of." Razin added: "and what he has no knowledge of, and what the prophets and angels were unable to know." From al-Rabiʿ the same is related, with the addition: "By Allah, Allah did not place in any star the life of anyone, nor his provision, nor his death; they only fabricate lies against Allah and make excuses by the stars." This was mentioned by the author of Jami al-Usul. The discussion refuting what the astrologers claimed has already passed in detail, so recall it. Perhaps something of that will come later, God willing. It is also permissible that all of these be taken to refer to the winds, for they, as they scatter, and what they scatter, stir up the clouds and carry them, flowing through the air with ease, and distributing the rain by directing the clouds to the regions. The reliance is upon what was related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, hearing it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and what the gate of the city of knowledge, may Allah honour his face, said from the pulpit. To this, as has been reported from al-Zajjaj, all the commentators, meaning the authoritative ones, have gone. The statement of the Imam after quoting it from the Amir: "The closest view is that bearing these four attributes on the winds is a great audacity, not to be accepted, and an ignorance of what Ibn al-Musayyab related, a report indicating that this is the interpretation of the Prophet (ﷺ)." Where is the Imam compared with ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him?

The statement of the author of al-Kashf: "It is highly suitable to the context, and for this reason the Imam preferred it," I do not accept for him either, if the hadith is sound. Then, if these attributes are taken to refer to different, distinct matters, as in the view relied upon, then the fa' (then) indicates order in the oaths both in mention and in rank, according to the gradation of their levels in indicating the perfection of His power, Mighty and Majestic. This gradation is either ascending or descending, since each of them has attributes which make it higher in one respect and lower in another when viewed by a sound observer. It has been said that the order is by reference to what is nearer to us and then what is nearer. If, however, all are taken to refer to one thing, namely the winds, then the order is that of the actions and attributes, for the wind first scatters the vapours into the air until they coalesce into cloud; second, it carries it; third, it moves with it, spreading and driving it to where Allah Most High commands, and then it distributes its rain. It has been said that if al-Dhariyat and al-Hamilat are taken to refer to women, then the apparent sense is that they differ in the indication of the perfection of power; so reflect.

The accusative of ﴿dharwan﴾ is as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), and ﴿wiqran﴾ is as a direct object (maf'ul bihi). Al-Imam permitted that it be of the type of "I struck him with a whip" (where the instrument is the object). ﴿Yusran﴾ is an attribute of an elided verbal noun with an elided genitive, meaning gliding with ease, or it is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning made easy, as related from Sibawayh. ﴿Amran﴾ is a direct object and is the singular of "affairs"; the singular is used for the plural, and it was not expressed in plural because the singular suits the rhyme endings, along with the clarity of the matter. It has been said that it is a circumstantial accusative, meaning commanded, with the direct object elided, or the attribute is treated as an intransitive, meaning that they perform the distribution commanded. Abu ʿAmr and Hamza read ﴿wa-l-dhariyati dharwan﴾ with the assimilation of the taʾ into the dhal. It is also read "wiqran" with a fatha on the waw, as a verbal noun of waqara, meaning to carry, as the words of al-Zamakhshari indicate, and sufficient is he as an imam in the language. Accordingly, it is also an object in the sense of the thing carried, or an absolute object of al-hamilat, as if it were said: "then the carriers carry a load."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verses 5–6:

His, exalted is His majesty, saying: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾ ﴿and indeed the Recompense (al-Din) is certainly going to occur﴾ is the answer to the oath. (What) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah) and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: indeed that which you are promised, or "you are promised with it." It is also possible that it is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), meaning: indeed your promise or your threat. In al-Kashshaf: it is a true promise, like ﴿a pleasant life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21]. (Al-Din) is the recompense, and its occurrence is its taking place. Most scholars hold that the thing promised is the Resurrection (al-Ba'th). In singling out the things mentioned for swearing by them, there is an allusion to their testifying to the realization of the proposition sworn to, inasmuch as they are wondrous matters; so whoever is able to create these is able to bring about the promised Resurrection.

﴿By the sky, full of paths﴾: i.e., the *ṭuruq* (paths). It is the plural of *ḥabīkah*, as in *ṭarīqah*, or of *ḥibāk*, as in *mithāl* and *muthul*. It is said that the water was *ḥubuk* (folded, rippled) by the flowing ripples when the wind passed over it. On this is the verse of Zuhayr describing a pond:

*Crowned with the roots of the stars, a wind from the north weaves it, for the morning light of its water has *ḥubuk*.*

The hair was also *ḥubuk*, due to the marks of its curling and its wrinkling. This interpretation is related from Muqatil, al-Kalbi, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk. What is meant by it is either the sensible paths along which the stars travel, or the intelligible paths which are perceived by insight, namely what indicates the oneness of the Creator, His power, His knowledge, and His wisdom, exalted is His majesty, when the observer contemplates them. Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, and al-Rabīʿ said: *dhāt al-khuluq al-mustawī al-jayyid* (possessing a level and good creation). In another narration from Mujāhid: *al-mutqanah al-bunyān* (of firmly made structure). It was also said: *dhāt al-ṣafāqah* (possessing firmness/solidity). These sayings are close in meaning. It seems that *ḥubuk* in these senses derives from their saying:

*ḥabaktu al-shay’* (I wove/tightened the thing), meaning *aḥkamtuhu* (I made it firm) and *aḥsantu ʿamalahu* (I did its work well); *ḥabaktu al-ʿuqdah* (I tied the knot), meaning *awthaqtuhā* (I made it secure); and *faras maḥbūk al-maʿāqim* (a horse with well-knit joints), where *maʿāqim* means the joints, i.e., well-fitted at them.

In *al-Kashf*: the root of *ḥabākah* is *ṣafāqah* (firmness) and goodness of the trace/texture. From al-Ḥasan: *ḥubukuhā* means its stars. The apparent view is that applying *ḥubuk* to the stars is metaphorical, because they adorn the sky as a woven garment is adorned by its woven pattern (*ḥabkuhu*) and the lines of its embroidery (*ṭarāʾiq washyihi*). So it is as if it were said: "possessing stars which are like *ḥubuk*, i.e., the lines in adornment."

As for *al-samāʾ* (the sky), it has been preferred that it is a collective noun, and by it is meant all the heavens. That each one of them is *dhāt ḥabk* in the sense of being level in creation and good, or of firm structure, or solid, or possessing intelligible paths is apparent. As for each of them being so in the sense of possessing sensible paths, this is by consideration that the stars, in whichever heaven they are, travel parallel to the rest of the heavens, so their courses, with regard to parallelism, are paths. And in the sense of possessing stars, this is by consideration that the stars, in whichever heaven they are, are visible in the rest of the heavens, based on the view that the heavens are transparent, so none of them blocks the perception of what lies behind it.

Ibn Manīʿ related from ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face, that he said: "It is the seventh heaven." And from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr the same. So reflect upon this and do not be heedless.

Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan (with a variant from him), Abū Mālik al-Ghifārī, Abū Ḥaywah, Ibn Abī ʿAblah, and Abū al-Sammāl, and Nuʿaym from Abū ʿAmr, read *al-Ḥubki* with the *bāʾ* sukūn, on the pattern of *al-qufl* (lock). ʿIkrimah read it with the *bāʾ* fatḥah, as the plural of *ḥubkah*, like *ṭarfah* and *ṭarf*, *barqah* and *baraq*. Abū Mālik al-Ghifārī and al-Ḥasan (with a variant from him as well) read it with *kasrah* on the *ḥāʾ* and *bāʾ*, like *al-ibil* (camels). According to what al-Khafājī mentioned, this is a singular noun that came on this pattern irregularly, and it is not a plural. Abū Mālik, al-Ḥasan, and Abū Ḥaywah also read it with *kasrah* on the *ḥāʾ* and sukūn on the *bāʾ*, like *al-silk* (thread). This is a lightening of a form with *kasrah* on the first and second letters, and it is a singular noun, not a plural, because the pattern *fiʿil* is not among the patterns of plurals; this was said by *al-Baḥr*. Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Mālik also read it with *fatḥah* on both, like *al-jabal* (mountain). Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī said: "It is the plural of *ḥubkah*, like *ʿuqbah* and *ʿuqab*." Al-Ḥasan also read it with *kasrah* on the *ḥāʾ* and *fatḥah* on the *bāʾ*, like *al-niʿam* (blessings). Abū Mālik also read it with *kasrah* on the *ḥāʾ* and *ḍammah* on the *bāʾ*. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah mentioned this reading from al-Ḥasan as well, then said: "It is an irregular reading, not well-founded." It seems that after he made the *ḥāʾ* *kasrah*, he imagined the reading of the majority, so he put a *ḍammah* on the *tāʾ*. This is one of the mixings of dialects, and this pattern does not exist in the speech of the Arabs, because it involves moving from lightness to heaviness, contrary to the pattern *ḍaraba* in the passive form. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: "It is unparalleled in Arabic in its patterns and forms, and I do not know what lies beyond it," and so ends his words.

On the basis of this mixing of dialects, the grammarians interpreted this reading. Abū Ḥayyān said: "In my view, the best is that this is among the cases where the vowel of the *ḥāʾ* is made to follow the vowel of the *tāʾ* of *(dhāt)* in the *kasrah*, and the unvowelled *lām* is not counted, because the unvowelled letter is a weak barrier."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, you are in a contradictory saying.﴾ That is, you are in conflict and contradiction regarding the command of Allah, mighty and majestic, in that you say that He, exalted is His majesty, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and yet you assert the validity of worshipping idols alongside Him, glorified is He. And regarding the command of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, you say at one time that he is a madman, and at another that he is a sorcerer, though a sorcerer is none other than a sane person. And regarding the matter of the Resurrection (hashr), you say at one time that there is no resurrection and no life after death at all, and at another you claim that your idols are your intercessors with Allah, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection, and so on, with other contradictory statements concerning that which they were commanded to believe in. Some scholars limited the "contradictory saying" to what concerns the command of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The clause is the answer to the oath (jawab al-qasam). Perhaps the point of that oath is to liken their sayings, in their divergence and the mutual opposition of their aims, to the paths of the heavens in their distance from one another and the variety of their forms; or it is an indication that their sayings are not sound and good, or not strong and firm, or that there is nothing in them that adorns them, but rather there is in them what disfigures them, namely contradiction.

﴿Whoever is turned away from it is turned away﴾. That is: he is turned away from belief in what he was commanded to believe in, given that the preceding discourse indicates it. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "from the Messenger (ﷺ)." Others said: "from the Qur'an." The preceding discourse implies every one who turns away, with the turning away that has no greater or more severe form. The intensification (mubalaghah) in ascribing the verb to the one described with it is as follows: were it not for the aim of intensification, it would be stating the obvious. It is as if another turning away were attributed to the one turned away, since it is said: ﴿He will be turned away from it﴾ [al-An'am: 16], the one turned away. So the intensification comes from the doubling, and then the unrestricted (ilaq) wording in a rhetorical context has a role in strengthening the matter of doubling. Likewise the indefiniteness in the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), which is close to His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Then there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78]. It was also said: the intended meaning of ﴿will be turned away from it﴾ is in external existence, from ﴿so he turned him away from him﴾ [Yusuf: 34], in the knowledge of God and His decree, glory be to Him. This was objected to on the ground that it has little benefit, because everything that exists is known to be established in God's eternal prior knowledge, and it does not contain the earlier intensification. The first objection was answered: it contains an indication that God's conclusive proof regarding his turning away is sufficient, and that suffices as a benefit. This is based on the principle that knowledge follows the known, so understand it. Al-Zahrawi related that the pronoun may refer to ﴿what you are promised﴾ or to "the religion." God, may He be exalted, swore by the scattering winds (al-Dhariyat) that the occurrence of the matter of the Resurrection is true. Then He swore by the sky that they are in ﴿a discordant saying﴾ regarding its occurrence; some of them are doubters, and some of them are deniers. Then He, majestic and exalted, said: ﴿is turned away﴾ from affirming the matter of the Resurrection, whoever is the one turned away. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned this without attributing it. The author of al-Kashf claimed that it is more apt for the coherence of the discourse. It was also said: the pronoun may refer to "a discordant saying," and "from" is for causation, as in His saying: ﴿We will not abandon our gods on account of your saying﴾ [Hud: 53], and his saying:

They are forbidden from eating and from drinking, like the wild cows that graze in abundance.

That is: because of that discordant saying, whoever wishes to embrace Islam is turned away. Al-Zamakhshari said: its literal sense is that their lie issues from the discordant saying. This is possible if "from" keeps its original meaning of transitivity, with the consideration of implicit meaning (tadmin); but it involves departing from the apparent meaning without need, along with the loss of that intensification. Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted the pronoun to refer to the saying, but he said: the meaning is that one is turned away from that discordant saying by God's granting success to Islam to whomever His happiness has overcome. This was objected to on the ground that it contradicts custom, since if the usage of "ifk" (lying/turning) is known as turning from good to evil, then you will find it only in those who are blamed. Furthermore, this is on the view that the address in "innakum" is to the disbelievers, which is what Ibn Zayd and others held; Abu Hayyan preferred that it is general to the Muslim and the disbeliever. Generality was also preferred in what preceded. The discordant saying is then the saying of the Muslims affirming the truth of the Messenger (peace be upon him), and the saying of the disbelievers to the contrary. Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah read "man ufika," with the verb in the active voice, meaning: whoever the people are turned away from it, and they are the Quraysh. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "yu'faku 'anhu man ufika," meaning: the people are turned away from it by one who is a great liar. It is also read "yu'fan 'anhu man ufin" with the letter nun in both, meaning: he deprives whoever is deprived, from afannah al-darʿa, when he exhausts the udder by milking it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 10:**

﴿Killed are the conjecturers (al-kharrasun)﴾, i.e., the liars among the people of the divergent speech. The origin of *al-kharṣ* (conjecture, guessing) is supposition and estimation, and it was then used figuratively for lying, because it is usually the source of it. Al-Raghib said: The reality of that is that every statement made on the basis of supposition and estimation is called *kharṣ*, whether it corresponds to the thing or contradicts it, insofar as its speaker did not say it on the basis of knowledge, nor of a predominant opinion, nor of hearing, but relied on supposition and estimation, like the act of the one who estimates the fruit when he estimates it. Anyone who speaks a statement in this manner may be called a liar, even if his statement corresponds to what was reported, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 1], and the verse. End of quotation. There is a discussion in this. The reality of *al-qatl* (killing) is well known, and what is meant by *qatl* here is the invoking of curses upon them, setting aside the literal meaning.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that he explained it as cursing. Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning of killing here is cursing, because whoever God Most High curses is in the position of one who has been killed and destroyed.

It was also recited as *qatlu al-kharasina* (قَتْلُ الخَراصِينَ), meaning: God has killed the conjecturers.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verses 11–12:**

﴿Those who are in a flood﴾ (ghamrah), in great ignorance, which overwhelms and encompasses them as water that covers what is in it covers it. ﴿Heedless﴾ (sahun), unmindful of what they were commanded. So the intended meaning of heedlessness (sahw) is absolute unmindfulness (ghaflah).

﴿They ask﴾, meaning, by way of hastening, mockingly, ﴿When is the Day of Judgment?﴾ The phrase ﴿ayyana yawmu al-din﴾ is the object (ma'mul) of ﴿yas'aluna﴾, treating it as analogous to "yaqulun" because of the sense of saying it contains. Alternatively, it is the object of an implied verb of saying, meaning: so they say, "When is the occurrence of the Day of Recompense?" The word "occurrence" (al-wuqu') is supplied so that the question concerns the event, as is well known with ﴿ayyan﴾. There is no harm in treating time as a time-bound thing, for the day, once it is made a promise and an awaited event, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So await the day when the sky will bring forth a visible smoke﴾ [al-Dukhan: 10], becomes attached to time-bound things. Likewise every day that has a matter of its own, such as the day of the festival (al-'id) and Nowruz (al-Nayruz). This is customary in the usage of both the Arabs and the non-Arabs (al-'Ajam). This is permissible according to the Ash'aris (al-Ash'ariyyah), that time may have a time, as has been detailed in its proper place.

It was also read as «iyyana» with a kasra on the hamzah, and this is a dialect (lughah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 13:

﴿On the Day they will be tormented over the Fire.﴾ That is, they will be burned. The root meaning of fitan (trial, torment) is the melting of a precious metal so that its adulteration becomes apparent; then it was used for burning, torment and the like. (Wa-yawma) is in the accusative of time (zarfiyyah) governed by an omitted element indicated by the fact that the speech occurs as an answer to a question; it is an annexation (mudaf) to the nominal clause after it. That is: the Day of Judgment occurs on the day they are over the Fire, etc. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a time-adverb governed by an omitted element that functions as the predicate of a similarly omitted subject, i.e., it is occurring, or existing, on the day, etc. It is also permitted that it itself be the predicate of an omitted subject, and the fatha is a fatha of indeclinability (bina') due to its annexation to something other than a noun, namely the nominal clause, since clauses are by origin of this type, according to a discussion between the Basrans and the Kufans detailed in the commentary on al-Tashil. That is: it is "the day they are over the Fire," etc. The pronoun has been said to refer to the time of occurrence, so this statement serves as the answer, in the manner of "They will say: 'To Allah'" as the answer to "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" (al-Ra'd: 16), because the implied question is "at what time will it occur?", whose original answer is "on such-and-such a day"; and if you say "at the time of its occurrence, on such-and-such a day," it serves in its place.

It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to the Day, and the speech is an answer in meaning; so the implied sense is "the Day of Recompense, the Day of the torment of the disbelievers." This is supported, as to its being in the nominative position as predicate of an omitted subject, by the reading of Ibn Abi Abla and al-Za'farani: "Yawma hum" with damma. Some grammarians claimed that "yawma" is an apposition (badal) to "Yawm al-Din," and its fatha in the reading of the majority is a fatha of indeclinability. (Yawma) and what is in its scope are part of the speech of the questioners, who said it mockingly; and it is related in terms of meaning. Let me correct that: the text is as follows.

In the commentary of al-Hadi it is stated that some grammarians permitted it absolutely, and some permitted it only with the adverbial complement, owing to its latitude, and they cited as evidence the line: "We have never been in need of your bounty" (nahnu 'an fadlika ma istaghayna). Unless it is claimed that whoever holds this view says that it was established in the Law. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ata' that he said concerning the verse: "That was when they were commanded to keep the whole night vigil, and Abu Dharr used to lean on a staff. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 19:

﴿And in their wealth there was a due right﴾, that is, a substantial portion which they imposed upon themselves, seeking nearness to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and out of compassion for the people. It is other than the zakah (obligatory almsgiving), as Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said.

﴿For the beggar﴾, the one who asks from them, ﴿and the deprived﴾, who is the one who abstains from asking (al-mutaʿaffif), whom the ignorant person thinks to be rich, so he is denied charity by most people.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Hibban and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The poor person (miskin) is not the one who is turned away by a date or two dates, or a morsel or two morsels.' It was said: 'Who then is the miskin?' He said: 'The one who does not have enough to make him independent, and whose condition is not known so that charity may be given to him. He is the deprived (mahrum).'"

Ibn Abbas explained it as the one who is afflicted (al-muharif), who seeks worldly provision and it turns away from him, and he does not ask people. It was also said: he is the one for whom the attainable means of provision are kept away from him after being near to him, so deprivation befalls him. Zayd ibn Aslam said: he is the one whose produce has been destroyed. It was said: the one whose livestock has died. It was said: the one who has no share in Islam. It was said: the one whose wealth does not grow. It was said: other than that. Al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) said: all of these are by way of illustration, and the sayings may be gathered into one: he is the one who has no wealth due to a deprivation that has befallen him. And I say in agreement with the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: this due right is the obligatory zakah. This was objected to on the basis that the surah is Meccan, whereas the obligation of zakah was in Medina. It was said: the origin of the obligation of zakah was in Mecca, and what was in Medina was the well-known measure of today. It is narrated from Ibn Umar that a man asked him about this right, and he said: "It is zakah, and besides that there are rights," thus generalizing. The majority hold the first view.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 20:

﴿And on the earth are signs﴾ — proofs from the varieties of minerals, plants and animals; or aspects of indication from the spreading out of the earth (al-dahw) and the elevation of some of it above the water, and the difference of its parts in qualities and properties. So the proof for the first (reading) is what is on the earth of existing things, and the particle of "in" (al-zarfiyyah) is real, and the plural is on its apparent sense. For the second (reading), the proof is the earth itself, and the plurality is by consideration of the aspects of indication and its states, and the "in" (al-zarfiyyah) is of the zarfiyyat al-sifah fi al-mawsuf (the indwelling of an attribute in the thing described), and (it indicates) the existence of the Creator, may His majesty be exalted, His knowledge, His power, His will, His oneness, and His abundant mercy, mighty and majestic is He. ﴿for those who have certainty﴾ — for the monotheists who have followed the upright, demonstrative path that leads to knowledge; they are beholders with seeing eyes and penetrating understandings. And Qatadah read (it) as "āyah" (in the singular).

The signs in the selves are more than can be counted. It has also been said: what is intended is the difference of tongues, shapes, colors, and natures, and this is narrated by ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās. The discourse is then according to an elided genitive (muḍāf), or metaphorically, by considering the existence of the causes in them as the existence of what they cause. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 23:

﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾. This is on the basis that the pronoun in (innahu) refers to (ma), and according to what preceded, it refers either to the provision (rizq), or to God Most High, or to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to the Qur'an, or to the religion in (inna al-din la-waqi'un) [al-Dhariyat: 6], or to the Day mentioned in ﴿When is the Day of Judgment?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 12], or to everything mentioned. As for the sayings, Abu Hayyan preferred the last of them, and it is related from Ibn Jarir, meaning that all that we have mentioned from the beginning of the surah until here is the truth ﴿like your speech﴾, i.e., like your speaking, just as there is no doubt for you that you speak, you should not doubt the truth of that. This is like the saying of people: "Indeed this is true, just as you see and hear." (Mithla) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun hidden in (haqqun), and it is not definite by being put in apposition, because of its extreme indefiniteness; or it is in the accusative as an attributive of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., "it is truly true, like your speech." It is also said that it is built on the fatha, so al-Mazini said:

Because it is compounded with ma until they became one word, like "woe to you" (waybuma).

They cited, as evidence for its being built together with ma, the words of the poet:

"Is it a bull I hunt for you, or two bulls, or is it your hornless one with two horns?"

Another said: it is built because it is attached to a non-declinable word, which is ma when it is an indefinite qualified noun meaning "thing," or a relative pronoun meaning "who." (Annakum) etc. is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., it is (annakum) etc., and the clause is an attribute or a relative clause, or it is (anna) with what follows it if ma is taken as extra; this is the explicit statement of al-Khalil. Its place, given the building, is nominative, being an attribute of (haqqun) or a second predicate. This is supported by the reading of Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'mash, with a variant from three of them: (mithla) in the nominative. In al-Bahr it is stated that the Kufans make (mathalan) an adverb of place and put it in the accusative as such, and they permit "Zayd mithluka" with the accusative; and on this basis it may be permitted that in the reading of the majority it is accusative as an adverb of place. Their argument and the response to them is mentioned in the grammatical works. In the verse there is an emphasis on the truth of what is mentioned that is not hidden. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that he said concerning it: It has reached me that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "May God fight a people to whom their Lord swore and yet they did not believe." And from al-Asma'i: I was coming from the mosque of Basra when a Bedouin appeared on a she-camel and said: "Which man are you?" I said: "One of the Banu Asma'." He said: "From where have you come?" I said: "From a place where the speech of the Most Merciful is recited." He said: "Recite to me." So I recited ﴿By the scatterers﴾, and when I reached ﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾ he said: "Enough." Then he rose to his she-camel and slaughtered it and distributed it, and he went to his sword and bow and broke them, and departed. When I performed the pilgrimage with al-Rashid, I began to circumambulate, and behold, someone was calling me with a gentle voice. I turned, and behold, it was the Bedouin, emaciated and yellowed. He greeted me and asked me to recite the surah. When I reached the verse he cried out and said: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true." Then he said: "Is there anything else?" So I recited ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾. He cried out and said: "Glory be to God! Who has angered the Majestic, so that He swore, and they did not believe Him by His word, until they forced Him to an oath!" He said it three times, and his soul departed with it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 24:

﴿Has there come to you the story of the guests of Abraham?﴾ In it is an exaltation of the status of the story and an alert that it is not among the things the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew except through revelation. So said more than one scholar. In al-Kashf, there is an allusion in it that when he (ﷺ) had finished establishing the recompense (al-jaza'), in wording for the oath and in meaning through what is in the sworn-by thing of the allusion to perfect power, with the truthfulness of the one who conveys (al-muballigh) folded into it, and had satisfied his need from its detail (mahhada) for the establishment of prophethood, and that this one who comes, truthful, deserves to be followed because of the dazzling miracles he has, then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Has there come to you﴾ etc. Included in it is consolation for him (ﷺ) concerning the denial of his people. So for him, with all his fathers and brothers among the prophets (peace be upon them), there is a good example (uswah hasanah). This is if ﴿And in Musa﴾ is not taken as coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying, glorified is He, ﴿And on the earth are signs﴾. As for on that assumption, its aspect is that the story of the Friend (al-Khalil) and Lut (peace be upon them both) is a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah) for consolation, by the removal of his deniers, and that he is one who is shown mercy, saved, honored with election, like his father Abraham (may the blessings of Allah, exalted is He, and His peace be upon him and upon them). The preponderance is with the first, ended. Soon, if Allah, exalted is He, wills, what is connected to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿And in Musa﴾ will come. And (the word "dayf" (guest) is originally a verbal noun (masdar) meaning inclination, and for this reason it is applied to the singular and the plural. It was said: they were twelve kings. It was said: three, Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil (peace be upon them). They were called "guests" because they were in the form of guests, and because Abraham (peace be upon him) supposed them to be such. So the naming is according to what appears and what is supposed. He began with the story of Abraham, although it is later than the story of 'Ad, because it is stronger in the purpose of consolation. ﴿The honored﴾, that is, with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as al-Hasan said. So it is like His saying, exalted is He, concerning the angels (peace be upon them): ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 26]. Or, with Abraham (peace be upon him), when he served them himself, along with his wife, and hastened their hospitality, and raised their seats, as is in some reports. And Ikrimah recited "al-Mukarramin" with shaddah (al-mukarrameen).

﴿When they entered upon him﴾ is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) modifying the narration, because it is originally a description (*sifah*). It may also modify "the guests," or "the honoured ones" (*al-mukramin*) if the honouring of Ibrahim is intended, since God's honouring of them is not restricted. Or it is in the accusative by an implied verb: "remember" (*udhkur*). ﴿So they said, "Peace"﴾: that is, "We greet you with peace," *salaman*. Abu Hayyan, in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*), held that deleting the verb is obligatory, because the verbal noun (*masdar*) stands in its place, so it is among the verbal nouns whose verbs must be omitted. Ibn ʿAtiyya said:

"It is possible that *salaman* is governed by *qalu* ('they said'), on the basis that it is treated as having the sense of *qawlan* ('a saying'), and the meaning would then be that they said a greeting and a saying, whose meaning is *salam*." This was attributed to Mujahid, but it is not that (sound).

﴿He said, "Peace"﴾: that is, "Upon you be peace." It was changed to the nominative by being a subject (*mubtada'*), to indicate permanence, so that his greeting would be better than theirs, out of added courtesy and honour. It has also been said that *salam* is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject, meaning "my affair is peace." Both are read in the nominative. It is also read *salaman qala silman* with a kasra on the sin, a sukun on the lam, and the accusative, where *silm* means *salam*. Ibn Wathhab, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Jubayr and Talha read *salaman qala silmun* with the kasra, sukun and nominative, and Abu Hayyan took it to mean "we are, or you are, peace."

﴿A people unknown﴾: he (peace be upon him) did not recognise them, because of the greeting that is the sign of Islam, or because they, peace be upon them, were not among the people he knew, or because their appearance and forms were different from the people's customs. *Qawmun* is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject, and most hold that the implied meaning is "You are a people unknown." He (peace be upon him) said this to them to get acquainted, like your saying to someone you meet, "I do not know you," meaning "Make yourself known to me and describe yourself." Some verifying scholars held that what appears is that the implied meaning is "These are a people unknown," and that he (peace be upon him) said it to himself, or to those with him among his followers and servants, without making them aware of it, for this is most suitable to his state

(peace be upon him), because addressing a guest with such words would cause some discomfort, and his asking them to make their state known might not remove that. Also, had he meant this, they would have revealed their conditions at the mentioned saying, and he (peace be upon him) would not have busied himself with the preliminaries of hospitality.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 26:

﴿So he turned quietly to his household﴾, meaning he went to them secretly, away from his guests. Abu Ubayda reported that one says راغ (rāgha) only when one goes off in secrecy. He also said: one says رَوَغَ اللُّقْمَةَ (rawagha al-luqmata) when he dips the morsel in ghee until it is soaked. Ibn al-Munir said: this is from the same meaning, because the morsel is taken away dipped in ghee so that it is hidden. From the inverted form of al-rawgh come ghawr al-ard (the depression of the earth) and al-jurh (the wound), because of their concealment, and the rest of its inverted forms are close to this meaning. Al-Raghib said: al-rawgh is inclination by way of cunning, and from it comes rāgha al-tha'lab (the fox tricked), and rāgha fulān ila fulān means he inclined toward him to obtain something he wanted from him by cunning. From this it is known that the secrecy was specified as a qualification by consideration, and this is also what the context requires, because whoever goes to his household to procure food usually goes in this manner. The fa' (فَ) indicates that he (peace be upon him) hastened to go and was not delayed. They have mentioned that it is part of the etiquette of the host to hasten to serve his guest without the guest noticing, out of concern that the guest might prevent him, or that he might become one who is kept waiting.

﴿So he brought a calf﴾, which is the young of a cow. It was named thus as if to suggest its youth (عِجْلَة, ʿijla), which is lost from it once it becomes a bull. ﴿fat﴾, meaning full of body with fat and meat. One says سَمِنَ (samina), like سَمِعَ (sami'a), سَمانَةً (samāna) with a fatha, and سَمْنًا (samnan), like عِنَبٌ (ʿinab), so he is سامِنٌ (sāmin) and سَمِينٌ (samīn). Like حَسَنٍ (ḥasan), the samīn is so by creation, as is stated in al-Qamus. In al-Bahr it is said: one says سَمِنَ سَمَّنا (samina sammanā), so he is samīn, an irregularity in the verbal noun, and the active participle and the regular forms are سَمِنَ and سَمَنَ. They also said سامَنَ (sāmana) when fat came to him. End.

The fa' here is فَصِيحَة (fasīha, the "eloquent" fa'), which reveals clauses that have been omitted, trusting in the situation to indicate them, and to signal the completion of the speed in bringing the food. The meaning is: so he slaughtered a calf, roasted it (فَحَنَذَهُ, fa-ḥanadhahu), and brought it. Some said that it had been prepared beforehand as roasted meat for whoever would visit him among the guests, so there is no need to estimate what has been mentioned. The well-known view today is that slaughtering for a guest when he arrives is more eloquent in honouring him than bringing what was prepared before his arrival. It was, as reported from Qatada, that the general wealth of (peace be upon him) was cattle, and had he had meat more delicious than it, he would have honoured them with it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 27:

﴿So he brought it near to them﴾, that is, he placed it before them. In this there is evidence that among the honouring of a guest is that more is offered to him than he will eat, and that food is not placed in one spot while the guest is invited to it. ﴿He said: "Will you not eat?"﴾ It has been said: this is an offer to eat, for in that there is an easing of the guest's mind. And it has been said: it is a rebuke for their not reaching out to eat. In some reports it is said that they said: "We do not eat except what we have paid its price for." So he (peace be upon him) said: "I do not permit it to you except for a price." They said: "And what is it?" He said: that you mention the name of Allah Most High at the beginning, and praise Him, Mighty and Majestic, at the end. Then some of them said to others: "Truly, He is the one whom Allah Most High took as a khalil (intimate friend)."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 28:

﴿So he conceived fear of them.﴾ He concealed within himself a fear of them when he saw that they did not partake of his food, and he thought that this was because they intended some harm. For a guest's eating is a sign of security and an indication that the host is at ease, and food carries a sanctity and a bond of protection, while refusing it is an estrangement that gives rise to the suspicion of evil. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that peace be upon him (ﷺ) felt in himself that they were angels sent for punishment, so he feared. ﴿They said: "Do not fear."﴾ "We are the messengers of Allah, exalted is He." It is reported from Yahya ibn Shaddad that Jibril, peace be upon him, touched the calf with his wing, and it got up running until it reached its mother, and so [Abraham] recognized them and felt secure from them. According to what is related from the Habr (Ibn 'Abbas), this was merely for the reassurance of [Abraham], peace be upon him. It was also said: [this occurred] together with his certainty that they were angels and their knowledge of what he had concealed within himself, either by Allah, exalted is He, informing them of it, or by the noble recording angels informing them of it, or by the manifestation of its sign on his noble face, so they inferred the inner state from it. ﴿And they gave him good tidings﴾ and in Surah al-Saffat (37:112) ﴿We gave him good tidings﴾, i.e., through them, ﴿of a boy﴾

He is, according to the majority, Isaac son of Sarah, and this is the correct view, for it is explicitly stated that he is the one promised in Surah Hud, and the story is one. Mujahid said: Isma'il son of Hajar, as Ibn Jarir and others narrated from him, but this hardly holds. ﴿Knowing﴾ when he reaches maturity and matures. In it is a promise of his long life. The good tidings were given with a mention of a son, because that is more consoling to the soul and more delightful. He was described with knowledge, because it is the attribute by which the perfect human being is distinguished, not beauty of form, strength, or the like. This is so according to other than the majority of the people of this age, for knowledge in their view, especially sacred knowledge, is a vice that no other vice equals, and ignorance is a virtue that no other virtue balances. In the intensive form together with the omission of the object there is what is not hidden, which necessitates joy. According to al-Hasan, ﴿knowing﴾ refers to a prophet. The good tidings came after reassurance, and in this is an indication that averting harm is more important than securing benefit. Some have mentioned that his peace be upon him knowledge that they were angels was from the fact that they gave him good tidings of the unseen.

﴿Then his wife came forward﴾, meaning Sarah, when she heard their glad tidings, [coming] to her house, and she had been in a corner, looking at them. In al-Tafsir al-Kabir (the Great Commentary of al-Razi), it is said that she had been serving them. When they spoke with her husband about her giving birth, she felt shy and turned away from them. So God, exalted is He, described that with the expression "coming forward" to the family, rather than "turning away" from the angels. If this is correct as a transmitted report and narration, the following address does not contradict it, since it requires only that she came forward and not that she turned away, for it suffices for its validity that it was within earshot of her, even if she was [still] occupied with household affairs. Yes, there is an antonymous metaphor (istiʿara diddiyya, a metaphor in which the word is used in the sense of its opposite) in the wording, and there is no indication here that supports it. It has also been said that "came forward" means "took," as you say, "he took to insulting me" (akhadha yashtumuni). ﴿in a loud cry﴾, meaning in a shriek of wailing (sarir), said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Qatadah and Ikrimah said: its ṣarra is its outcry. It has been said: it is her saying "awh" (an exclamation of distress). It has been said: her saying "O woe is me!" It has been said: "in intensity." It has been said: al-ṣurra is a group whose members are gathered close to one another, as if they had been bundled together, that is, collected into a container. Ibn Bahr went to this view and said: that is, she came forward in a group of women, rushing to look at the angels, peace be upon them. The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥal), or of a direct object if "came forward" is interpreted as "took." It has been said that the particle (fi) in it is superfluous, as in his saying: "it wounds in their hamstrings my blade," and the sense is "took a cry." It has been said, rather, that the prepositional phrase is in the position of the predicate, because the verb in that case is one of the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah, verbs indicating that an action is about to occur). ﴿and she struck her face﴾. Mujahid said: she struck her forehead with her hand and said: "O woe to me!" It has been said that she found the heat of the blood and slapped her face out of shame. It has been said that she slapped it out of astonishment, and that is the act of women when they are astonished at something. ﴿And she said: an old woman﴾, meaning, I am an old woman, ﴿barren﴾, meaning sterile, so how can I bear a child? ʿAqim is on the pattern faʿil; it has been said that it has the meaning of the active or the passive participle. The original meaning of ʿuqm is dryness.

**[Ruh al-Ma'ani, al-Alusi, on Surah 51, verse 30]**

﴿They said: "Thus says your Lord"﴾ — i.e., in the same manner as that noble word which He informed us of, ﴿"Your Lord said"﴾. We are only relaying it to you from Him, Exalted and Majestic, not saying it from our own selves. It is narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) said to her: "Look at the ceiling of your house," so she looked, and behold, its beams were green and fruit-bearing. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾. So the word of Him, Exalted and Majestic, is true, and His act, glorified be He, is perfect without doubt. This exchange did not take place with Sarah alone, but was also with Ibrahim, as has preceded in Surah al-Hijr. The reason it is not mentioned here is that it is sufficient with what was mentioned there, just as Sarah is not mentioned there, being sufficient with what was mentioned here and in Surah Hud.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 31–33:

﴿He said﴾ i.e., Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when he realised that they were angels sent for a matter, ﴿"Then what is your business, O messengers?"﴾ i.e., what is your great affair for which you were sent, other than the good news?

﴿They said, "We have been sent to a guilty people"﴾, meaning the people of Lut (peace be upon him), ﴿"that we may send down upon them"﴾, i.e., after overturning their towns upside down, as has been explained in the other noble surahs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 34:

﴿Marked﴾ (musawwamah): made distinctive, from al-sawmah, which is a mark. Upon each of them was the name of the one who would be destroyed by it. It was also said: they were informed that they were from the stones of punishment. It was also said: by a sign which indicates that they are not from the stones of this world. It was also said: musawwamah means sent forth, from asmat al-ibil fi al-mar'a (the camels pastured), and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And from it is trees in which you pasture [your livestock]﴾ [al-Nahl: 10]. ﴿With your Lord﴾ (inda rabbika), i.e., in the place where His power and His majesty, glorified is He, the Mighty and Majestic, are manifest. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun in order to censure them for extravagance after censuring them for criminality, and to point to the cause of the ruling.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 35:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So We brought out﴾ and so on, is a narration from Him, Exalted is He, of what befell the people of Lot, peace be upon him, in summary form, after the narration of the words exchanged between the angels and Abraham, peace be upon them both. The fa' here is the fa' of eloquent explanation (fa' fasiha), disclosing sentences that have been omitted, relying on their mention in another place. It is as if it were said: "They rose from him and came to Lot, and there passed between them and him what passed, and they carried out what they had been commanded. Abu al-Sammal, Mujahid and Ibn Miqsam read ﴿the sky﴾ and ﴿the earth﴾ in the nominative case, on the basis that they are subjects (mubtada') and what follows them is their predicate (khabar). ﴿And of everything﴾, that is, of every kind of living being, ﴿We created pairs﴾, two types, male and female. This is the view of Ibn Zayd and others. Mujahid said: this is an indication of opposites and correlatives, such as night and day, misery and happiness, guidance and error, sky and earth, blackness and whiteness, health and sickness, and so on. Al-Tabari preferred this view, on the ground that it is more indicative of power. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the logical genus (al-jins al-mantiqi), the least that can fall under it being two species. Thus, for example, God, glorified is He, created from substance (jawhar) the material and the immaterial; from the material, the growing and the inert; from the growing, the perceiving and the plant; and from the perceiving, the mute and the speaking. This, as you see, [is one view]. ﴿So that you may remember﴾, that is, We did all of that so that you would remember and recognize that He, mighty and majestic, is the Lord, the Powerful, whom nothing can overcome, and so that you would act according to its requirement and not worship anything other than Him. It has also been said: We created that so that you would remember and know that multiplicity is a property of contingent things (al-mumakkanat), and that the Necessary Existent in Himself, glorified is He, does not admit of multiplicity or division. It has also been said: the intended meaning is remembering all that has been mentioned in regard to the matter of the Gathering and Resurrection, because whoever is able to bring all that into existence is able to restore the dead on the Day of Resurrection; and this has a basis. Abi read ﴿you remember﴾ with two taa's and a lightened dhal.

**"So flee to Allah."** This is a consequence (tafri') of His words, "that you may remember" (﴿لَعَلَّكم تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾). It is an allegory (tamthil) for seeking refuge (i'tisam) in Him, glorified and exalted is He, and in His Oneness, mighty and majestic is He. The meaning is: say, O Muhammad, "Flee to Allah," because of the fact that "I am to you from Him" (﴿إنِّي لَكم مِنهُ﴾), that is, from His punishment, exalted is He, which is prepared for whoever does not flee to Him, glorified is He, and does not declare Him one, "a clear warner" (﴿نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ﴾), clear in that he is a warner from Allah, glorified is He, by means of the miracles (al-mu'jizat); or "clear" (mubin) means that he makes clear what must be warned against.

And do not set up another god alongside God; indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner. It is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with the command, and it is an explicit prohibition of associating partners with God, like the phrase "affirm His oneness and do not associate [anything with Him]." Among the transmitted remembrances is: "There is no god but God alone, with no partner." He repeated the statement "Indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner" because the first is linked to the command and this one to the prohibition. The purpose of all of this is to urge *tawhid* (affirmation of God's oneness) and to exaggerate in giving counsel. It has been said that what is meant by His saying, ﴿So flee to God﴾, is the command to faith and the constant maintenance of obedience. The mention of ﴿Do not set up another god﴾ and so on is singled out as the greatest thing from which one must flee. The statement "Indeed I am to you" and so on: the first is ordered upon abandoning faith and obedience, and the second upon associating partners. Thus they are distinct, because what each is ordered upon is distinct, and it came as a cause for it. However, this is not free of difficulty.

Al-Zamakhshari said regarding the verse: "Flee (to) His obedience and His reward from His disobedience and His punishment, affirm His oneness, and do not associate [anything] with Him." He repeated "Indeed I am to you" and so on at the command to obedience and the prohibition of association, so that it would be known that faith does not benefit except together with action, just as action does not benefit except together with faith, and that no one succeeds with God, exalted is He, except one who combines both. End of quote. But there is no indication in the verse for this in any way. Furthermore, his interpretation of fleeing to God in a way that applies to action alone is not acceptable. Even if the warning about abandoning action is granted, from where does it follow that it lacks benefit? The People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*) do not dispute that a warning has occurred for committing disobedience. What comes to mind, on the assumption that what is meant by fleeing to God is worship, is that He, exalted is He, first commanded it and threatened its abandoner with the threat known in the Law, which is punishment without eternal abiding. Then He, exalted is His majesty, prohibited secondly that anyone be associated with His worship, and the associator was threatened with the threat known for him, which is eternal abiding. On this basis the two threats are distinct, and the verse, in placing the command before the prohibition, is similar to His saying: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous work and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ [al-Kahf: 110], and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And worship God and do not associate anything with Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 36]. And where is this from what al-Zamakhshari mentioned? May God deal with him by His justice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 52:

﴿Thus﴾, that is, the matter is like this. It is an affirmation and emphasis of what has passed more than once. It is also from eloquent speech (fasl al-khitab, decisive and eloquent discourse), because when He, glory be to Him, wished to begin the story of their divergent saying about the Messenger, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, after it had been mentioned in general or specific terms in His saying, ﴿Indeed, you are in a varying saying﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 8], and after He had placed in between what He placed in between, He, glory be to Him, said: "The matter is like this," that is, like what is mentioned, and His report will come to you. Here ﴿thus﴾ refers to the speech that follows it, namely His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿There came not to those before them﴾ to the end of the verse. So this is an explanation of what was stated in summary. This is also the meaning of those who said: the reference is to their denial of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and their calling him, far be it from him, a sorcerer and a madman.

It is known from what has been mentioned that ﴿thus﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject (khabar mubtada' mahdhuf). Its being in the accusative as an adjective of its verbal noun (masdar) is not permitted, the verb being ﴿came﴾ (ya'ti). The reference is to the coming, that is, ﴿there came not to those before them﴾ any messenger with a coming like their coming ﴿except that they said﴾, etc. This is because what follows the negative ﴿ma﴾ does not operate on what precedes it, according to the well-known view. It also cannot be assumed as an implied verb under the condition of tafsir (explanatory verb), because what is not known cannot be explained as an operator in such a position, as the grammarians have stated explicitly. Some made it an object of ﴿they said﴾, with the reference being to the saying: "except that they said a sorcerer or a madman, a saying like that saying." This is also not permitted, even though it is a stretch, due to some ground.

The pronoun in ﴿before them﴾ refers to Quraysh, that is: those who came before Quraysh. ﴿From a messenger﴾ means a messenger among the messengers of Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿Except that they said﴾ concerning him: ﴿a sorcerer or a madman﴾, a predicate of an omitted subject, that is, he is a sorcerer. As for ﴿or﴾ (aw): it is said to be from the narration, meaning (except that they said, "A sorcerer," or they said, "A madman"), and it serves to prevent an empty alternative (li-man'i al-khuluww). It is not part of what is reported, so that the saying of each would be the whole of ("a sorcerer or a madman"). In al-Bahr it is for distribution (li-al-tafsil), meaning: some said, "A sorcerer," some said, "A madman," and some said, "A sorcerer and a madman." Thus the speakers are collected in the pronoun, and "or" indicates distribution. End. So do not be heedless.

The verse has been challenged on the ground that it indicates that no messenger came except that he was denied, whereas the messengers who confirmed the law of those before them, such as Yusha' (Joshua), peace be upon him, were not denied; and likewise Adam, peace be upon him, was sent and was not denied. The Imam [al-Razi] answered: "We do not concede that the one confirmed is a messenger; rather he is a prophet upon the religion of a messenger, and whoever denies his messenger denies him too." This was critiqued: the reports, and likewise the verses, indicate that those who confirmed were messengers. Moreover, the difficulty remains with Adam, peace be upon him, who himself acknowledged that he was sent and was not denied. Some answered the difficulty concerning those who confirmed (the law) by saying: the verse only indicates that all the messengers who came before them had things said about them, and this does not include those who confirmed, because the apparent meaning of a messenger's coming to a people is his coming to them without another having conveyed to them what the one before him brought. This did not occur for the confirmer of the law of the one before him, as is not hidden. As for the difficulty concerning Adam, peace be upon him, [the answer is] that the intended meaning is: those who came before them among the nations who existed in a manner similar to the existence of these, [there came not] a messenger to them except that they said, etc. Adam, peace be upon him, did not come to a nation like that, since at the time he was sent there was none but his wife, Hawwa'. Perhaps this is better than what was said: that the intended meaning of "a messenger" is a messenger from among the sons of Adam, so he, peace be upon him, is not included in that.

It was also challenged that ﴿except that they said﴾ indicates that they all were denied, whereas no messenger came except that a people believed in him. The Imam answered that attributing the saying to a plural pronoun is meant to refer to the many, indeed the majority, and the one who denies is mentioned alone because that suits the purpose of consolation. Some took from this the answer to the previous difficulty, saying: the judgment is based on what is generally the case, not that every nation to which a messenger came denied him, so that Adam and the confirmers are excluded since they were not denied, and in this there is what there is. Some interpreted ﴿those before them﴾ as the disbelievers, and by this they resolved both difficulties, and in this there is what is not hidden. So reflect on all of that, and do not assume that the answer is limited to what you have heard. Look carefully. And Allah, Exalted is He, is the Guide to the best of paths.

﴿Nay, but they are a transgressing people.﴾ This is a shift (idrab, a turning away) from the claim that mutual charging is what unites them, to the claim that what unites them upon that statement is their shared rebellion (tughyan) which drives them to it.

**Ruh al-Ma'ani of al-Alusi, commentary on Surah 51, verses 54–55**

﴿So turn away from them﴾: i.e., disregard their disputation, for the call has been repeated to them and you have spared no effort in making it clear. Yet they refused, persisting in refusal and obstinacy. ﴿You are not to be blamed﴾ for turning away after you have exerted every effort and gone beyond every customary limit in conveying the message.

﴿And remind﴾: the imperative *adim* (أدِمْ, "persist"), meaning: continue in the act of reminding and admonition and do not abandon it. The command to remind is for continuity in it, and the verb is treated as intransitive. It is also permissible that the object is omitted, i.e., "remind them," and it is omitted because the matter is evident.

﴿For the reminder benefits the believers﴾: i.e., those whom God Most High has predestined to faith, or those who are believers in fact, for it increases them in insight and strength in certainty. In al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit* of Abu Hayyan), it is said that the apparent meaning of the verse indicates a *mu'adah* (a truce or peaceful coexistence), which has been abrogated (*mansukhah*, i.e., naskh, abrogation) by the Verse of the Sword (*ayat al-sayf*). Abu Dawud, in his work on abrogation, and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas, regarding the words of God Most High ﴿So turn away from them﴾, etc., and he said: God commanded him to turn away from them so that He might punish them, and He excused Muhammad (ﷺ). Then He, glorified be He, said ﴿And remind﴾, etc., and this abrogated that.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah*, and a group, by way of Mujahid, from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, said: When ﴿So turn away from them, for you are not to be blamed﴾ was revealed, none of us remained but was certain of destruction, since the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to turn away from us. Then ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾ was revealed, and our hearts were content.

From Qatada: they thought that revelation had ceased and that the punishment had come near, so God Most High revealed ﴿And remind﴾, etc.
