﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) that emphasizes the command and confirms the content of its causal clause (ta'lil). Their creation is for what the Exalted has mentioned, which is what calls the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to remind them, and which makes it obligatory for them to take heed and be admonished. Perhaps the jinn are mentioned first because their creation preceded that of humankind in existence. The apparent meaning is that the intended reference is to those who are contrasted with them and with the angels (peace be upon them). The angels are not mentioned. It has been said that this is because the matter concerning them is settled. Or it is because the verse was brought to explain the conduct of the deniers, who abandoned the worship of God, the Exalted, though they were created for it. This abandonment does not occur among the angels; rather, they are honored servants who do not disdain His worship, may He be exalted and glorified. It has also been said that the Prophet (ﷺ) was not sent to them, so mentioning them in this ruling is not something that calls him (peace be upon him) to remind them. You know that the more correct view is the generality of the mission (bi'thah), so the first view, namely what was said in its place, is preferable, since they have no need of reminder and admonition.

It has been said that the intended meaning of "the jinn" is what covers them, because the word is derived from concealment (al-istitar), and they are hidden from humans. It has also been said that it is not valid to mention them within the domain of creation (al-khalq), because they are like spirits from the world of command (alam al-amr), which is contrasted with the world of creation (alam al-khalq). Both are indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿His is the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. This was countered by His saying, glorified be He: "Creator of all things" [al-An'am: 102; al-Ra'd: 16; al-Zumar: 62; Ghafir: 62], and ﴿His is the creation and the command﴾ is not as was supposed.

Worship (ibadah) is the utmost degree of submission. The apparent meaning is that what is intended by it is that which occurs by choice, not that which occurs by subjugation (al-taskhir), which is established for all created beings. The latter is the indication that draws attention to their being created and that they are the creation of a wise Agent. It is expressed by prostration, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [al-Rahman: 6].

The definite article in "the jinn and humankind" is, according to the well-known view, for comprehensiveness (istighraq). As for the lam (of purpose) in "li-ya'buduni," it has been said that it indicates the end-purpose (ghayah), and the worship is the end, even though it is not a purpose sought from the creation, because there is evidence that He, the Mighty and Majestic, did not create the jinn and humankind for its sake; that is, He did not will it from them. For had He willed it from them, it would not have been left unfulfilled, because the Divine will entails what is willed, as is explained in the books of principles (al-usul). Moreover, the observed fact is that it is unfulfilled. Also, the apparent meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind﴾ [al-A'raf: 179] indicates that the intention of sins from the many is that they deserve Hell thereby, which contradicts the will of worship. But since their creation was in a state fit for worship and prepared for it, in that He, glorified be He, put into them intellects and gave them outward and inward senses, and other aspects of preparedness, their creation was made to have this as its end, as an intensification, by likening what prepares a thing for something to the end of it. Such usage is common in custom. Do you not see that they say of a strong man's body: "He was created for wrestling," and of a cow: "She was created for plowing."

In al-Kashf: "The acts of Him, the Exalted, lead to perfective ends, and the lam in them is for that purpose. As for will, it is not a requirement of the lam except when it is known that the motive is desirable in itself. On this basis, no interpretation is needed, for they were created in such a way that worship is possible from them, and they were guided to it, and that was made a perfective end of their creation. The fact that some of them are prevented from reaching it does not prevent the end from being an end. This is a plain meaning." End of quotation. So reflect on it.

It has been said that the intended meaning of worship is humble submission through subjugation, and it is evident that all of them worship Him in that sense, without distinction between believer and disbeliever, righteous and wicked, and the like. Among what has been said: the meaning is "I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should humble themselves to My decree." It has also been said: the meaning is "I did not create them except that they might be servants to Me," and by "servant" is meant the servant by origination (al-abd bi'l-ijad), and the generality of the description applying to them is evident from His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93]. But it has been objected to this: that "abdan" in the sense of "became a servant" is not at all from the language.

It has also been said that worship means monotheism (tawhid), based on what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that every instance of worship in the Qur'an is monotheism. So all of them declare His oneness in the Hereafter. As for the monotheism of the believer in this world, it is there evident. As for the monotheism of the polytheist, it is indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then their trial was only that they said, "By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. Upon this is the saying of one who said: "No disbeliever enters the Fire." Or the intended meaning is, as al-Kalbi said: the believer declares His oneness in hardship and ease, while the disbeliever declares His oneness, glorified be He, in hardship and calamity, but not in blessing and ease, as He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Ankabut: 65]. It is not hidden after this that it is far from the apparent meaning and the context.

It is reported from 'Ali, may God ennoble his face, and from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that "I did not create them except that I might command them and call them to worship." This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They were not commanded except to worship God﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5]. So He mentioned worship, which is caused by command in the Law, or necessarily accompanies it, and its cause or what it necessitates is intended. This is a metonymy (majaz mursal). You know that the command to each individual of the jinn and each individual of humankind is not established, especially when they are not accountable, such as children who die before the time of accountability, who are included in the generality.

Mujahid said: the meaning of "li-ya'buduni" is "li-ya'rifuni" (that they may know Me). This is also a metonymy (majaz mursal), from using the name of the cause for the effect, according to what is in al-Irshad. Perhaps the secret in it is to draw attention to the fact that what counts is the knowledge gained through worshipping God, the Exalted, not what is attained by other means, such as the knowledge of the philosophers. It has been said: this is good, for if He, the Mighty and Majestic, had not created them, His existence and His oneness, glorified be He and exalted, would not have been known. And it has come in a hadith: "I was a hidden treasure, so I loved to be known, so I created the creation that I might be known." It was countered that true knowledge has not been realized in everyone, but in some who denied His existence, such as the naturalists today. Therefore the earlier statement must be affirmed in explaining the causal clause. Then, the report with this wording was mentioned by Sa'd al-Din al-Farghani in Muntaha al-Madarik, while others, such as al-Shaykh al-Akbar, mentioned it in the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter of al-Futuhat with another wording. The hadith scholars (al-huffaz) critiqued it. Ibn Taymiyya said: it is not a saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), and no sound or weak chain of transmission is known for it. Likewise al-Zarkashi, Ibn Hajar and others said. And whoever among the Sufis narrates it admits that it is not established by transmission, but says that it is established by unveiling (kashf). The Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, explicitly stated this in the chapter mentioned. Verification by unveiling is a habit of theirs. Nevertheless, there is a problem of meaning in it, though it has been answered in three ways that will come, God willing.

It has been said: "al-jinn and al-insan" the article is for prior reference (al-'ahd), and the intended ones are the believers, because of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly created﴾ — the verse — that is, based on the view that the lam there is not for the end-result (al-'aqibah). This view is attributed to Zayd ibn Aslam and Sufyan, and is supported by His saying, the Exalted, as it is said: ﴿For indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾. Abu Hayyan supported it with the report of Ibn 'Abbas from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I did not create the jinn and humankind except from among the believers," and some narrated it as a reading of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Among people, some made it for the genus, and said: it suffices for establishing the ruling for it that it is established for some of its individuals, and here they are the believing obedient ones, and this ultimately coincides with the preceding view. There is no difficulty in this view if the lam is taken as an actual desired end, and likewise if it is taken as purpose according to one who permits explaining God's acts by purposes while the essential self-sufficiency remains and there is no perfecting through another, as many of the early generations (salaf) and the later ones (muhdathun) held. I have heard that some of them divide will into legislative will (shar'iyyah), which concerns acts of obedience, and creational will (takwiniyyah), which concerns acts of disobedience and others. On this basis it is permitted to leave "the jinn and humankind" in their inclusion of the disobedient, and it is said that worship is also willed from them, but by legislative will. However, this is not complete unless this will does not entail the occurrence of what is willed, like the delegating will (al-irada al-tafwidiyyah), held by the Mu'tazila.

This is all. And if you have a sufficient grasp of the views on the interpretation of this verse, the removal of the apparent conflict between it and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they will not cease to differ﴾ ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them﴾ [Hud: 118, 119] becomes easy for you, on the assumption that the reference in that is to difference, by adopting some of those views in it. Some have repelled it by saying that the lam in that verse is for the end-result. What comes to mind is that the restriction (al-hasr) is relative (idafi), meaning: I created them for worship, not for its opposite, or not for seeking provision and feeding, as some of them indicated, taking it from the sequel to that in His saying, glorified be He:

﴿I do not desire any provision from them, nor do I desire that they feed Me.﴾ This shows that His manner with His servants is not like the manner of masters with their slaves. Masters own slaves so that they may be helped in obtaining their livelihoods and provisions. The Owner of all owners of slaves, may He be exalted and glorified, denied that His ownership of them is for that purpose. It is as if He, glorified is He, said: "I do not desire to be helped by them as the owners of slaves are helped by their slaves. So let them occupy themselves with what they were created for, which is My worship."

The Imam mentioned two aspects of this. The first is that it serves to dispel the assumption that God needs their worship because of their creation. The second is that it serves to confirm that they were created for it. He explained this by saying that in common usage an action must have some benefit. But slaves are of two kinds. One kind is acquired to display grandeur, by standing before their masters and honoring them, like the slaves of kings. The other kind is acquired to benefit from them in obtaining provisions or preparing them. So it is as if He, glorified is He, said: "I created them, and there must be some benefit in them. Let them reflect upon themselves: are they of the kind from whom the obtaining of provision is requested, when they are not like that? So I do not desire any provision from them. Are they among those from whom the preparing of food is requested, like the cook or one who brings food near? They are not like that." ﴿Nor do I desire that they feed Me.﴾ Thus they are slaves of the first kind, and so they should not abandon honoring Him.

The apparent meaning is: "I do not desire from them any provision for Myself," because of His words, glorified is He, ﴿nor do I desire that they feed Me.﴾ The Imam took this view.

He mentioned several subtle points about the verse:

The first is that He, glorified is He, repeated the negation of the two desires, because a master may ask a slave to earn for him, which is requesting provision, and may not ask it when he has abundant wealth, yet he asks that his needs be met, such as guarding his wealth and bringing food from his property before him. So the negation of the first desire does not necessitate the negation of the second, and so the denial was repeated, meaning: "I do not desire this, and I do not desire that."

The second is that the arrangement of the two negations, as the sublime wording includes, is a matter of ascending order in describing His self-sufficiency, may He be exalted and glorified. It is as if He said: "I do not ask them for provision, nor for what is less than that, which is bringing food before the master. For that is a matter that is often asked of slaves when earning is not asked of them."

The third is that He, glorified is He, said: "I do not desire from them any provision," rather than "I do not desire from them that they provide," because earning is for requesting a substance, not an action.

He, glorified is He, said: "nor do I desire that they feed Me," rather than "nor do I desire food from them," because this is an indication of independence from what a slave does who is not commanded to earn, such as a slave of abundant wealth who has no need for the action itself.

The fourth is that He, may He be exalted, singled out feeding for mention, because the lowest degree of seeking help is that a master asks his slave to prepare food. Negating the lower implies negating the higher by way of priority. So it is as if it was said: "I do not desire from them any substance or any action."

The fifth is that "mā" is for negating the present. However, what is meant by it is this world, and it is brought in as an allusion, not as a negation of the future, because it is clearly known that after his death a slave is not fit to be asked for provision or food. [End of quotation from his words.] So reflect on it.

From the apparent meaning of al-Zamakhshari's words, the meaning is: "I do not desire from them any provision for Me or for them." In al-Bahr: "I do not desire from them any provision," meaning that they should not provide for themselves or for others. ﴿Nor do I desire that they feed Me,﴾ meaning that they should not feed My creation. So this is by omission of a noun, as Ibn Abbas said.

Similar to this is what has been said: "The meaning is: I do not desire that they provide for anyone from My creation, nor do I desire that they feed him." The feeding is attributed to Himself, glorified is He, because all creation are the dependents of God, exalted is He. Whoever feeds the dependents of someone, it is as if he has fed that person.

In a hadith (a report from the Prophet ﷺ) it says: "O My servant, I was ill and you did not visit Me. I was hungry and you did not feed Me." Its ending indicates the meaning: "My servant was ill and you did not visit him, and he was hungry and you did not feed him."

It has also been said that the verse is governed by an implied "Say," so it has the same meaning as His words, glorified is He: ﴿Say: I do not ask you any wage for it﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. The third-person address in it is for preserving the narrative, since in such cases both third person and second person are permitted. It has been read both ways in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome﴾ [Al 'Imran: 12]. It has also been said that the meaning is: "Say to them, and concerning them," so the third person in "from them" and "they feed Me" fits this. This does not conflict with the reading "Indeed I am the Provider," which comes after, because in that case it is a reason for the command to speak or to comply, not for the absence of desire. Yes, there is no doubt that this is a very distant opinion.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 51, verse 58:

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider (al-Razzaq)﴾ who provides for everyone who is in need of provision, none other than Him, glory be to Him, whether independently or in partnership. From this is understood His exaltation, mighty and majestic, above needing provision. ﴿The Possessor of strength (dhu al-quwwah)﴾, i.e., of power (al-qudrah). ﴿The Firm (al-Matin)﴾, i.e., of intense strength. The clause is a justification for the absence of the will [to be provided for]. The Imam (al-Razi) said: His, exalted is He, being the Provider, relates to the absence of seeking provision, because whoever seeks it is poor and needy. His, mighty and majestic is He, being the Possessor of firm strength, relates to the absence of seeking the work intended by His words, glory be to Him: ﴿I do not desire that they feed Me﴾, because whoever seeks it is incapable and has no strength. It is as if it were said: I do not desire from them any provision, because I am the Provider, and I do not desire from them any work, because I am strong and firm. The apparent expression would have been "Indeed I am the Provider," as occurs in one reading attributed to him (ﷺ), but he turned to the third person, and the use of the august name is due to its being well known for the meaning of worship, so that this carries an indication of the cause of the ruling. Also, so that the verse comes out in the form of a proverb, as it was said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ [al-Isra: 81]. Expressing it in this manner, on the view that there is an implied "say" before what precedes, is the apparent meaning, and the other reading requires what we mentioned just above. Glory be to Him, He preferred "Possessor of strength" over "the strong." It was said: because in "dhu" (Possessor of), as Ibn Hajar al-Haytami and others said, there is glorification of what it is attributed to, and the one described by it; and the context requires it. For this reason "al-Matin" was brought after it, and it was not sufficient to dispense with the description by strength. The Imam said: since the purpose is to establish what has preceded, namely the absence of the will for provision and the absence of seeking help from others, the description of provision was brought in the intensive form, because without the intensive form it would not suffice to establish the absence of the will for provision; and the description of strength was brought without intensification, because it suffices to establish the absence of seeking help, for whoever has strength short of the utmost does not seek help from others. But since "Possessor of strength" indicates no more than that He, exalted is He, has some strength, the description "al-Matin," which is the One who has steadfastness that does not waver, was added. Then he said: the strong (al-Qawiyy) is more emphatic than the possessor of strength, and might (al-'Izzah) is more complete than firmness (al-Matanah). The more complete has been paired with the more complete, and what is less with what is less, in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers unseen. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. And in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider…﴾ etc., as the context required that. He has extended the discussion on this point, and I do not think it is free of turbidity. Ibn Muhaysin read "al-Razzaq" in the pattern of the active participle. Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read "al-Matini" in the genitive case, and it is construed as an adjective of "al-quwwah." This is permissible despite its masculine form, either because it is interpreted as "al-iqtidar" (power), or because it is on the pattern of verbal nouns, in which masculine and feminine are alike, or because it is treated as the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. Abu al-Fath permitted that it be an adjective of "dhu," and the genitive case by proximity (al-jiwar), like the saying "this is the burrow of a lizard that is ruined," but it is weak.

﴿So indeed, for those who wronged﴾: that is, if it is established that Allah, exalted is He, created the jinn and mankind only that they might worship Him, and that He, glorified is He, desires no provision from them, and so on through what has preceded, then indeed for those who wronged themselves by occupying themselves with other than that for which they were created, namely worship, and by associating others with Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and by denying His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), and they are the people of Makkah and their like among the disbelievers of the Arabs. ﴿a portion (dhanūban)﴾: that is, a share of the punishment. ﴿like the portion (dhanūb) of their companions﴾: that is, the share of their counterparts from the earlier nations. The root meaning of dhanūb (a portion, share) is a large bucket full of water, or one nearly full. Al-Jawhari said: "It is not called dhanūb when it is empty. It may be masculine or feminine, and its plurals are adhnibah and dhanā'ib." It was then borrowed for a share in general, whether bad, like the share of punishment in the verse, or good, as in the gift in the verse of Alqamah ibn Abadah al-Tamimi, praising al-Harith ibn Abi Shamir al-Ghassani, who had taken his brother Ash'as captive on the day of ʿAyn Abagh:

"In every tribe you have dipped with a blessing, so Ash'as has a right to a share (dhanūb) of your generosity."

It is reported that al-Harith, when he heard this verse, said: "Yes, and more shares (adhnibah)." Among its uses for a share is the saying of another poet:

"By your life, while the deaths are visiting, each of the sons of one father has a share (dhanūb) of them."

This is a common usage. In al-Kashshaf, this is an illustration of its original sense among water-carriers who divide the water, so that this one has a bucket (dhanūb) and that one has a bucket (dhanūb). The reciter (al-Rajiz) said:

"Indeed, when a stranger comes upon us, he has a bucket and we have a bucket,
and if you refuse, then the well (qalīb) is ours."

﴿So let them not seek to hasten Me﴾: that is, let them not ask me to hasten its coming. It is said: "He asked him to hasten (istaʿjalahu)," meaning he urged him to haste and requested it from him. It is also said: "I sought the hastening of such-and-such (istaʿjaltu kadhā)" if I requested that it occur quickly. From this is the verse: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [An-Nahl: 1]. According to al-Irshad, this is a response to their saying: ﴿"When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48; al-Anbiya: 38; an-Naml: 71; Saba: 29; Ya-Sin: 48; al-Mulk: 25].

[p. 25]

"So woe to those who disbelieve" (﴿فَوَيْلٌ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾). That is, "so woe to them." Placing the relative pronoun (al-ladhina) in the position of their pronoun serves to brand them with the disbelief contained in the relative clause and to indicate the reason for the judgment. The fa' (so) indicates that woe is established for them as a consequence of their having a great punishment, just as the fa' before it indicates that the prohibition against hastening is a consequence of that. The min (from) in His words, glorified is He, ﴿مِن يَوْمِهِمُ الَّذِي يُوعَدُونَ﴾ ("from their day which they are promised"), is causal (li-l-ta'lil). The returning pronoun to the relative pronoun is omitted, meaning "they are promised it" or "they are promised with it," according to one view. The day referred to is said to be the Day of Badr, and this is preferred because it better fits what precedes it, in that it consists of punishments from the worldly torment. It is also said to be the Day of Resurrection, and this is preferred because it is more suitable to what is at the beginning of the following noble surah. And God Most High knows best.

Among what some of the people of allusion (ahl al-isharah, Sufi esoteric interpreters) have said regarding some verses: "By the scatterers scattering" (﴿والذّارِياتِ ذَرْوًا﴾) is an allusion to the winds that carry the moans of the yearning ones, who are exposed to the breezes of subtle kindnesses, to the courts of might; then they bring the fragrance of the breezes of the Truth to the nostrils of the lovers, so they find a rest from the overpowering of the burning of longing. "And those that carry burdens" (﴿فالحامِلاتِ وِقْرًا﴾) is an allusion to the clouds of the subtle kindnesses of divinity, carrying the rains of the mercies of lordship, so they rain upon the hearts of the sincere. "And those that run with ease" (﴿فالجارِياتِ يُسْرًا﴾) is an allusion to the ships of the hearts of the lovers that run with the winds of care upon the sea of tawhid (unity of God), in the easiest of states. "And those that distribute by command" (﴿فالمُقَسِّماتِ أمْرًا﴾) is an allusion to the angels descending from the enclosures of holiness with glad tidings and knowledges upon the hearts of the people of steadfastness. And if you wish, you may make the whole an allusion to kinds of winds of care, of which some carry the hearts into the atmosphere of the unseen. The passionate lover (al-'ashiq al-majazi) has said:

"Take from the breeze of Najd a security for its heart,
a breeze whose fragrance nearly flies off with its mind.
And beware of that breeze, for indeed
whenever it blows, the passion becomes easier in its affair."

Among them, "those that carry burdens" is the remedy for the hearts of the lovers, as has been said:

"O two mountains of Nu'man, by God, leave
the breeze of the morning to reach its breeze.
I find its coolness, or a heat in me burns
upon a liver of which nothing remains but its core.
Indeed the east wind is a wind which, when it breathes
upon the soul of one grieved, its griefs are dispelled."

Among them, "those that run" are from the breezes of the sacred presences (hadarat al-quds) to the hearts of the people of intimacy with ease, to revive their hearts. Among them, "those that distribute" are what they bring of what has been perfumed for them from the traces of the Divine Presence upon the souls of those prepared, according to their preparations. And if you wish, say other than that; the door is wide.

"By the sky with its folds" (﴿والسَّماءِ ذاتِ الحُبُكِ﴾) is an allusion to the sky of the heart, for it has paths to God, Mighty and Majestic.

"Indeed the righteous will be in gardens and springs" (﴿إنَّ المُتَّقِينَ في جَنّاتٍ وعُيُونٍ﴾) is an allusion to the gardens of union and the springs of wisdom.

"And at dawn they seek forgiveness" (﴿وبِالأسْحارِ هم يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ﴾): they seek ghafr, that is, the covering of their existence by the existence of their Beloved; or they seek forgiveness for the sin of seeing their own worship, from the beginning of the night until dawn.

"And from everything We created pairs" (﴿ومِن كُلِّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْنا زَوْجَيْنِ﴾) is an allusion to the fact that all that is seen manifest among existents is not a true unity; rather it is composite, and at least it is composed of possibility (imkan), and something else. The true One is none but God Most High, whose reality is His very being (aniyyah), glorified is He.

"So flee to God" (﴿فَفِرُّوا إلى اللَّهِ﴾) by abandoning all other than Him, Mighty and Majestic.

"And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me" (﴿وما خَلَقْتُ الجِنَّ والإنْسَ إلا لِيَعْبُدُونِ﴾): that is, "to know Me" (liya'rifun). This, according to them, is an allusion to what they have affirmed as sound through unveiling (kashf), from the narration of the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, from his Lord, glorified is He, that He said: "I was a hidden treasure, so I loved to be known, so I created creation that I might be known."

In the book al-Anwar al-Saniyya of al-Sayyid Nur al-Din al-Samhudi, with the wording: "I was a hidden treasure, so I loved that I should be known, so I created this creation that they might know Me, and by Me they knew Me." In al-Maqasid al-Hasana of al-Sakhawi, with the wording: "I was a treasure not known, so I created a creation and made Myself known to them, so they knew Me." And other than that.

This is problematic, because hiddenness is a relative matter, so there must be something hidden and something hidden from. Where there is no creation, there is nothing hidden from which hiddenness is realized. It is answered, first, that the hiddenness is from the fixed entities (al-a'yan al-thabita), because things in their fixed state have no existential perception; so God, glorified is He, was hidden from them, not known to them with existential knowledge. So He loved to be known with a knowledge that is newly arisen from an existent that has come into being; so He created creation, because their existential knowledge is a branch of their existence. Thus He made Himself known to them through kinds of manifestations, according to the differences of their preparations, and they knew themselves through the manifestations, and thereby they knew God Most High; so through Him, glorified is He, they knew Him.

Second, that what is meant by hiddenness is its consequence, which is that no one knows Him, Mighty and Exalted. This is confirmed by the wording of al-Sakhawi, "I was a treasure not known" (la a'rifu), in place of "hidden" (makhfiyyan).

Third, that "makhfi" means "manifest," from akhfahu, that is, "he made it manifest," the hamza being for removal, that is, "he removed its hiddenness." The ordering of His words, glorified is He, "so I loved that I should be known," etc., upon this is on the basis that manifestation, when it is strong, necessitates ignorance of the state of the manifest; so God, glorified is He, created creation so that they would be like a veil, and thereby knowledge becomes possible. Do you not see that the sun, because of its intense manifestation, most eyes cannot stand to look at its state except through placing some veils between it and them? This, as you see, is not free from discussion.

As for the application of "treasure" (kanz) to Him, Mighty and Majestic, it has been transmitted. Al-Daylami related in his Musnad from Anas, raised to the Prophet: "The treasure of the believer is his Lord" (kanz al-mu'min rabbuhu), that is, because from Him, glorified is He, comes everything precious that he attains in both abodes. And Shaykh Muhyi al-Din, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned in the meaning of "treasure" something other than that, saying in the three hundred and fifty-eighth chapter of his Futuhat: "If there were not in the world one who is in the image of the Truth, the purpose of knowledge of the Truth would not have been achieved, namely the knowledge of the originated, in his saying: 'I was a treasure...' etc. So He made Himself a treasure, and a treasure is only a treasure while being hoarded in something. So the treasure of the Truth was not Himself except in the image of the Perfect Man in the thingness of His fixed reality there. The Truth was hoarded. When the Truth clothed the Human Being with the garment of the thingness of existence, the treasure appeared by its manifestation, and the Perfect Human Being knew Him by His existence, and knew that He, glorified is He, had been hoarded in him in the thingness of His fixed reality, and he was not aware of it." End of quote. And this is the "Speech of the Birds" (mantiq al-tayr), which we do not know. We ask God Most High for success in what He loves and is pleased with, by His grace and generosity.
